subject: hydra
pitch:
Category: Monster.
Subject: five-headed hydra.
Style: God of War.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for a five-headed hydra creature in a God of War aesthetic—dark, battle-scarred, bronze-and-iron armored with glowing eyes and rune markings—and need to design its rigged skeleton, rest pose, named joints, and jaw structure while keeping the overall scope manageable.

Now I'm sketching the actual proportions and bone hierarchy: a spine chain running from hips through chest where the necks branch off, a thick curving tail off the hips, and four stout quadruped legs using limb IK to reach the ground, all with coordinates roughly scaled to a 4.5m long body.

For 3-segment legs, I'll need 4 named joints: hip, knee, hock, ankle. I'm deciding front legs stay 2-segment while hind legs get 3-segment digitigrade chains, naming left/right sides by X-position sign, then moving on to building five necks as separate joint chains extending from the chest.

Now I'm working out how the five necks fan outward from the chest, each with different lateral spread and height so the central neck stands tallest, curving S-like paths with heads angled slightly outward to avoid overlap.

For the skeleton, I'm setting up chains per neck with named joints and a separate head joint parented to the neck's final segment, so I can control head orientation independently from the neck's path tangent.

Now I'm planning the head's internal structure per creature: skull, upper snout, a separately-jointed jaw, teeth, horns/crest, glowing eye decals, nostrils, brow ridges, and frills or spines, all built through a dedicated head-construction function.

For the overall visual language, I'm leaning into a God of War aesthetic -- dark scarred scales with ember-lit cracks, bronze and iron armor bands, broken chain-shackles around the necks, torn pauldron fragments, and rune-carved bands drawn as custom SVG paths rather than relying on font-based text rendering.

Now I'm planning out the texture set: a glowing amber reptilian eye decal, a rune-engraved bronze band texture, an ember-glow claw scar decal for the flanks, a frill spine blade with a dark-to-ember gradient, and a banded belly plate texture.

Beyond those, I'm considering glowing crack lines for the back, chain links built from alternating torus geometry, and a Greek key meander pattern for collar trim. For the base paint, I'm defining a mixed hide shader combining scale patterns with countershading and moss/soot mottling.

Writing custom paint logic...

Writing custom paint function...

I'm also planning a neck variant of the hide paint with lighter throat plates banded along the sweep direction using sine-based striping.

Checking that `s` is passed into the paint function as the third parameter, good. For armor, I'll pull metal paints from the clockwork kit—bronze with tarnish and verdigris for collar bands, iron for chains—and double-check the correct import paths from the builder library and its kits.

Now I'm working out the body geometry: setting the hip joint position, then building the spine as a catmull-rom chain running from hips up through the chest, with the torso sized as a wide barrel shape sitting at roughly waist-to-chest height.

I'm also planning the tail chain extending backward from the hips, curving downward along a similar catmull-rom path through several descending points.

I'm deciding to keep the torso and tail as separate sweep operations rather than one continuous tube, matching their radii near the junction so the tail base blends into the torso's rear with minimal visible crease, even though the hips joint technically sits outside the spine chain itself.

Now I'm working out the torso's radius function across its length, tuning a sine-based formula so the chest end stays broad instead of tapering to a point — I need to adjust the curve since the current math narrows too much at t=1.

Fine-tuning the width and height functions with gaussian-like peaks centered on the chest and belly, adding a downward shift so the belly sags naturally, and settling on using 10-sided cross sections for a slightly smoother low-poly look. Now I'm figuring out where the neck bases attach onto the torso's top surface near the chest region.

Working out the fanning layout for multiple necks branching off the chest joint, with base positions spread laterally and sunk slightly into the torso, then defining per-neck parameters like height, lateral spread, and forward extension that scale with how far each neck is from center.

Still working out the neck curve equations...

Still working out neck path points...

I'll switch to using underscores to separate the label from the number so names stay unambiguous, like "neck_L1_1" through "neck_L1_5". For the head itself, I need to set up its local frame so forward, right, and up align with the bone direction rather than raw model axes.

With the tilt roughly consistent, I can use numeric local coordinates where x is right, y is along the bone, and z is up, placing parts directly in head-local axes. Using `frame: head` lets geometry inherit the bone's orientation automatically, so I can build shapes in head-local space and position them with a moved point relative to that frame.

Boxes use width/length/height for x/y/z, spheres use scale, and I'll pass bone explicitly for safety since explicit bone always wins over frame. For mirrored features I'll flip geometry x-coordinates by sign rather than relying on orientation, keeping rotation as a fallback for tilted asymmetric pieces like cones since orientation priority goes quat, aim/dir, rotation, then frame.

Since rotation and frame orientation can't combine directly, I'll rotate geometry beforehand with a helper rather than trying to layer rotation on top of frame placement. For horns, teeth, and spikes, the cleanest approach is using rod/sweep with explicit bone and points generated via head.local, which sidesteps the orientation conflict entirely.

For the broader skull and snout shapes, I'm uncertain whether loft produces a circular or box-like cross-section, so rather than risk unexpected geometry I'll fall back to sweep with a variable radius function along a path, since that behavior is well-defined.

Planning the skull-to-snout sweep now, deciding on an 8-sided cross-section for a slightly faceted but still rounded look, and sketching the head-local path coordinates from the back of the skull to the nose tip with radii tapering appropriately.

I'll add a helper function to interpolate radius profiles from keyframes, then set up the lower jaw as a separate joint attached to the head with its own sweep path and tapering radii, plus teeth geometry.

Since the closed mouth hides any interior, I'll add a subtly glowing ember-red tongue rod on the jaw, and pose each head's jaw open at varying small angles (8-18°) so fangs peek out differently across heads.

I need to confirm poses are applied after building so the rigid jaw sweeps rotate correctly with the joint, and work out the right axis sign — positive rotation about local X should tip the forward-pointing jaw bone downward to open the mouth, accounting for the head's own yaw.

For the eyes, I'm placing decals with the skull sweep as the target surface, figuring out the outward and forward-facing direction vector for each eye socket position.

Since a hit also sets dir to the surface normal, I want the eye oriented with forward-facing predator intent rather than purely outward, so I'll blend the hit normal with a forward vector weighted toward the front for that slanted, reptilian look. I'm aiming for an ember-glowing iris with a black slit pupil and a heavy, angry brow, drawn slightly asymmetrically for a menacing feel.

I'm working through the geometry carefully: which eye is the creature's right versus left as seen from the viewer, and how the mirror flag in the decal system flips the drawing to generate the opposite eye. Getting the slant direction wrong would make the brows read as sad rather than angry, so I'm reasoning through the convention that the default decal represents the creature's right eye, with mirror:true producing the left eye on the positive side.

I'm also checking whether glow works correctly on decal parts with transparent regions and standard material textures, and deciding to stick closely to documented SDK behavior rather than attempt anything exotic, since I can't actually test these calls and want to minimize risk of subtle failures.

Let me mentally review the builder API I'm relying on: joint, chain, sweep, part, stick, surface, extrude, lathe, spike, rod -- making sure I'm using each with signatures that match what's documented rather than guessing at undocumented options.

Now I'm sketching out part budgets for a five-headed creature: per head roughly 14 teeth-plus-jaw parts (merging teeth geometry where sensible to keep counts manageable), plus horns, brow ridges, eyes, nostrils, and frill blades, aiming for a total somewhere in the 180-340 part range.

I'm tallying it out further: ~30 parts per head (150 total), neck throat plates and armor bands (~50), legs with claws and armor (~48), tail (~20), back spikes (~20), chains, and ember crack decals, landing around 300 parts total with triangle counts comfortably under the 60k soft limit. I'm setting up helper functions for vector creation and keyframe-based profile interpolation to drive the sweep geometry.

Now I'm figuring out teeth: rather than importing mergeGeometries from BufferGeometryUtils, I'm considering just using individual cone-shaped spike parts per tooth, but that balloons part count fast — 24 teeth per head across 5 heads would add 120 parts, pushing the total toward 450, over my target range. I'm trimming each jaw down to 4 teeth per side (8 upper, 8 lower, 16 per head, 80 total) to stay within budget, while also weighing whether to merge each jaw's teeth into a single geometry using the addons utility to cut part count further.

I can use the SDK's `aim` helper to build a quaternion pointing toward a direction vector and apply it to the geometry, then translate into position, with flat shading enabled on the part. For orientation, upper teeth should angle downward and slightly forward while lower teeth angle upward, placed along the jaw edges accordingly.

I'm now working out the exact head geometry constants—defining local coordinates in "head units" and a scale factor per head (center, side, outer), with a helper that multiplies every local point and size by that scale so I can lay out the skull, snout, and jaw consistently across different head sizes.

Still defining jaw geometry...

Since the jaw sits inside the snout, it reads as if they're one merged volume, so I'm adjusting the jaw's center and radius to create a visible mouth line separating it from the snout.

Still checking jaw-skull overlap at each cross-section to make sure the jaw stays tucked under the skull along the snout length.

Placing the teeth positions now — upper fangs angled downward with a larger central fang, lower teeth and tusks angled upward near the jaw tip, each with slightly varying length and radius for a natural look.

Now I'm figuring out the horns: curved sweeps from the back of the skull using bezier control points with tapering radius, attached to the head bone, with different horn styles varied per head for visual diversity.

I'm also planning per-head config options, assigning crown-style horns to the central head and ram/spike horns to side heads, then adding brow ridges as rods sloping down toward the center to give an angry expression above each eye socket.

For the eye decal, I need to orient it along the outward-forward direction so it sits naturally on the side of the head. Then for nostrils, I'm placing small dark spikes near the snout tip hit point, plus adding a nose ring.

For the frill, I'm designing a blade-shaped outline for crest spines behind each skull, placed as a fan plus a ring of spine blades around the neck near the head.

Writing blade placement logic...

For extrusion, I'd pass tangent and normal as the x and y axes, keeping them perpendicular so the blade rides the tube's bones rigidly rather than inheriting a blended frame. To lean the blade backward, I can tilt the y-direction by mixing the normal with a bit of negative tangent, though I need to check whether extrude actually requires strict orthogonality or just uses the cross product for thickness.

Working through the trig, I derive that y = n·cosθ − t·sinθ and x = t·cosθ + n·sinθ keeps the two axes perpendicular for any lean angle θ, which solves the shearing issue — now I need to figure out how dorsal angle zero maps to world-up for the torso plates.

For the neck restraints, I'm planning iron bands as closed ring paths swept around the neck at each point, sampling the neck radius function at parameter t to size the ring before using catmull interpolation and sweep to build the chain geometry.

Since the point carries its bone reference already, I can just pass the neck point directly and the rigid band will follow whichever bone dominates there. I'm now thinking about placing several bands along the neck at different t values to form an armored collar, maybe bronze plates with a Greek key pattern, though the lathe shape only supports solid color so texture would need another approach.

For texture I'll use the paint function to generate a Greek key or riveted pattern based on height and angle, or simpler, just apply a panelled bronze metal finish with tarnish and rivets for a quick armored look. For the dangling chains, I'm picturing a broken shackle on the foreleg and a chain hanging from the neck band, built by threading alternating torus links along a curved path.

Still working out chain link orientation...

I like the idea of a shackle on the right forefoot with a trailing chain to a broken link on the ground, evoking the chained-beast motif. Writing the catmull curve path for the chain's draping trajectory...

Beyond that, I'm leaning toward embedding broken spears and scarred, armored hide details into the hydra's design to match a God of War aesthetic—weathered bronze, rune carvings, battle damage rather than anything floating or ornamental.

I'll keep the spearhead mostly hidden inside the body, showing just the shaft with a broken splintered tip, a bronze ring band, and a rag tassel for detail. For textures I'm planning a glowing reptilian ember eye and a rune-carved band for bronze plates, likely using textured decal planes since extrude geometry only takes solid paints.

I'm placing glowing cursed runes as decals on the torso flanks and neck bases to look like branded binding seals, then adding diagonal ember-lit claw scar decals on shoulders and heads, and ember crack textures on the back—possibly merging these scar variants together.

I'm also planning frill cards along the neck sides using a spiky tuft texture with a dark-root-to-ember-tip gradient, scattered across the upper neck sweep, plus a tattered cloth banner card with meander trim hanging from a spear shaft.

I'm considering extra Greek-flavored details, like a broken bronze hoplon shield with a lambda emblem embedded in a flank for extra texture, though I'm weighing whether this adds too much complexity.

So I'm tallying the texture set I'll need: eye, runes, claw scar, crack, spike card, rag, emblem, maybe a teeth grin too. Now I need to be careful that every SVG string is valid markup so it doesn't throw a parser error when loaded as a texture.

Writing eye SVG markup...

Still drawing rune glyphs...

Still writing SVG shapes...

Now I'm pinning down the actual skeleton coordinates: hips, spine path points, torso radius, and where the legs attach relative to the ground plane.

Checking hind leg distances similarly, about 1.64 against a segment sum of 2.35, so I'm setting bend directions with the knee forward and hock back to keep it anatomically plausible, then structuring the chain as hip, knee, hock, ankle points for each leg.

For the front legs with three points I'm naming them shoulder, elbow, wrist, with the ankle/wrist acting as the tip joint parenting the foot. I'm also planning the paw as a flattened shape sitting under the ankle, centered around y≈0.1 so it just touches the ground contact plane near y=0.

Now I'm working out leg sweep radii, tapering thickness from a thicker thigh/shoulder down to a narrower wrist/ankle using arrays of radius values keyed along the chain, with hind legs getting a bigger thigh bulge than front legs.

For feet, I'm planning the toes as short capsule sweeps fanned forward from the ankle/wrist joint, with claw tips, parenting them to the foot joint position and spacing toe bases slightly apart along x and z for a natural splay.

For leg armor, I'm adding bronze greaves and cuffs lathed around the lower leg at a specific joint position, plus a shackle-and-chain on one front leg, and considering a domed pauldron plate on the shoulders using a lathed half-sphere for scattered armor fragments.

Placing the pauldron domes on both shoulders as rusted bronze with rivets, finding the shoulder surface hit point and orienting the lathe profile along the surface normal so it embeds naturally into the body.

I'm positioning the neck bases and shoulder pauldrons outside the neck width, then sketching the tail as a chain of points curving backward and downward from the hips across seven spans.

The tail tapers from a thicker base near the body to a thin tip resting on the ground with a slight curl, and I'm considering giving the end an arrowhead or bone-blade shape rather than a plain point.

Checking proportions overall: with five heads around 5 meters high and a tail roughly 5-6 meters long, the full creature would stretch close to 11 meters, which feels appropriately massive for a hydra. I'll trim the tail length slightly so it doesn't push the total scale too far.

Now I'm setting head heights so the center head towers over the two flanking pairs, with necks tapering from a thicker base near the shoulders out to thinner tips, and spacing the heads laterally so they fan outward from the torso for a convincingly multi-headed silhouette.

I'm defining the radius taper array along each neck chain, placing the neck base just inside the torso so it visibly emerges around the shoulder line, then sweeping a smooth skin mesh over the chain and adding throat plate decoration as colored sectors along the belly side of the neck.

Now I'm adding a bony spike crest down the top of each neck, lathe-cut bronze bands wrapping around partway up, and scattering small spiny cards along the sides—accounting for the texture-per-mesh output across all five necks.

For the bands, I'm calculating neck radius at each sample point via interpolation, then orienting the lathe along the neck's local tangent so it follows the sway. I'm sketching a closed ring profile with five points to give the band a slightly flared, concave cross-section.

I need to pad the ring's radius so it clears the neck's polygonal circumscribed edge rather than clipping into it, so I'm computing inner and outer radii with a small margin added to the base neck radius. Then I'm moving on to torso adornments, starting with dorsal plates distributed along the torso's spine with varying blade sizes.

Since the necks occupy the front-top of the torso, I'm restricting the dorsal plate row to the lower/back portion of the torso sweep, avoiding overlap with the neck bases. After that I'm planning belly plating, ember crack decals on the flanks and back, scar decals on the shoulders, rune seals on the flanks, plus spears, a shield, and pauldrons.

For the decals, I'm placing them by finding the nearest surface point on the torso near the flank position, then using that hit's normal as both the placement direction and orientation, with a default world-up vector for alignment.

Now I'm adding a personality touch: a claw-scar decal across one head's face, overlapping the eye, which gives me the idea of giving that head a blind, milky-white eye instead of the normal glowing iris. I'm thinking I'll need a separate eye texture variant for this — maybe writing an eyeSvg function that takes color stops so I can generate different eye looks (ember orange for most heads, a pale blind variant for the scarred one) and cache them for reuse across heads.

Tallying textures and materials now: three eye variants plus runes, claw marks, cracks, spikes, rags, and emblem brings me to nine textures total, and I'm defining the paint palette for hide, neck, skull, jaw, bronze, iron, wood grain, and a horn material that needs a gradient from dark base to pale bone tip.

Still writing paint definitions...

For the mouth, I'll make the interior a deep red tone, deciding to skip any ember glow for simplicity. I want to keep the overall palette tight, staying within a flat-color budget of 64 colors total.

Now I'm setting up the imports, pulling in the geometry utilities, the custom builder helpers, and clockwork/glow kits I'll need to construct this scene, while checking which helper functions are actually exported from the main SDK module.

I should be careful about unused imports and parameters since typecheck may flag them, so I'll only import what I actually use and type things loosely with `any` where I'm unsure, since this likely gets transpiled without strict checking.

Defining color palette constants for the hydra design...

Still writing hide paint logic...

Still writing shading logic... I'm reconsidering whether banding should be driven by a different coordinate for necks versus legs, since the current approach looks off on rising neck geometry.

Writing shaft colors...

I need to fix the profile function's return type to a proper tuple, then I'm building a tail chain from a catmull-rom spline with six segments parented to the hips, naming each segment tail1 through tail6.

Still refining tail geometry...

Writing blade outline shape...

Actually simpler to just shift the base points down slightly rather than touching the bone data, avoiding the complexity. Now I'm working out blade shading, using a paint function that gradients color by position along the length, from dark near the root to a bone-white tip with a glowing ember edge.

I'm realizing I should share a single blade paint across all blades rather than baking a new one per instance, since each painted part consumes texture resolution from a shared sheet, and having too many unique paints would degrade quality given the large total painted surface area across torso and necks.

So I'm estimating texel density across the whole body (roughly 130 m² of painted surface), which comes out coarse at 1024px but improves noticeably by bumping the paint sheet to 2048 or allowing the atlas up to 4096. For the blades specifically, I'm deciding flat colors would be cheaper than a full gradient paint, though I'll keep a shared paint since it's simple enough. Now moving on to legs.

Writing leg-building logic...

For the front legs I should also use the "leg" role rather than "arm" since this is a quadruped, with contact points placed at floor level under each foot. Tracing through the spine joint positions, spine4 sits at z=1.0, matching the shoulder position, so that's index 3 and the correct parent for both the front legs and the neck.

The hind hips at z=-1.2 fall between spine1 and spine2, so I'll parent them to the hips joint instead. For sweeping the legs I'm defining radii arrays that taper along the chain—thicker at the shoulder/hip and narrowing toward the foot—using round caps so the foot pads blend smoothly. I'm also adding a small sphere bulge at the shoulder joint to suggest muscle definition, scaled slightly to fit the body proportions.

Now I'm working on the foot geometry: a flattened palm sphere positioned so its bottom sits right at ground level, plus three toe capsules spreading outward from the foot tip with slight z-offsets for a natural splay, and claw spikes attached to each toe tip.

I'm also adding a dew claw spike at the wrist and then setting up the hind leg chain, checking that segment lengths and target positions keep the IK solvable given the hip and ankle placement.

For the hind legs I'm naming the joints hip, knee, hock, and ankle, thickening the radii for a sturdier look, and planning extra toe pads plus a backward spur. I'm also figuring out foot placement for a digitigrade stance and thinking about where to attach bronze greaves along the front leg chain.

I want a reusable cuff function that lathes a bronze ring around any point on a limb chain, plus helper functions to interpolate radius values along a leg for consistent tapering. Now I'm setting up the configuration for each head on the neck—defining per-head traits like height, forward offset, length, head scale, eye color, and horn style for each of the five heads (R2, R1, center, L1, L2) arranged outward from the body.

Working out neck path building...

I'm computing the head direction as a slightly downward-pitched normal vector, then blending that with the final path tangent to make the neck's endpoint curve smoothly into the head orientation.

The direction shifts sharply near the final segment, curving the neck into an arch so the head droops down and forward, like a swan looking down menacingly. I'm tallying up the total neck length from the rise and forward curve, then working out the final head position in 3D space.

Now I'm checking where the heads land for the outer figures, making sure the lateral offsets angle them slightly outward while still facing forward, and verifying none of the heads collide with each other given their x and z coordinates.

I'm also sizing the neck radius taper along the chain so it shrinks smoothly toward the head, then setting up five neck joints per side and attaching the head joint to the end of that neck chain with the proper direction and role.

The head joint uses its local frame with the right axis chosen as close to the creature's right side as possible, so I can define other head-relative points consistently.

Setting up the head-building function with local point helper...

Still writing head geometry...

Refining the ridge placement...

I want to use surface hits to seat things properly against the skull mesh, so I'll grab a single surface reference and query nearest points for each feature instead of guessing coordinates. For the "crown" horn type, I'm sketching symmetric pairs of swept horns rooted at hit points near the rear top, curving backward and tapering in radius.

Now I'm adding a secondary cheek spike per side using a short spike primitive aligned to the hit's normal, then working through "ram" horns as curling catmull-rom paths that spiral outward and forward for each side.

Still writing spike placement logic...

For "swept" I'll do long straight sweeping blades like antelope horns using a three-point catmull curve. For "broken" I'm considering one intact horn paired with a snapped stump capped in bronze, maybe with a small chain loop ring attached.

Now I'm placing jaw-side spikes (three per cheek) and working out brow ridge geometry as a swept bone shape, with the inner end sitting lower than the outer end to approximate a natural slope above the eyes.

Still working out the brow sweep...

Adding eye decal logic...
